body: Dumping un-sanitized user data into HTTP adapters is asking for trouble. Similar [features are offered by ext/curl](http://php.net/manual/en/book.curl.php) which is why it was implemented the way it was.

It's a bad idea in cURL as well, which is why it is now deprecated: http://php.net/manual/en/function.curl-setopt.php
As of PHP 5.5.0, the @ prefix is deprecated and files can be sent using CURLFile. The @ prefix can be disabled for safe passing of values beginning with @ by setting the CURLOPT_SAFE_UPLOAD option to TRUE.
In vanilla PHP, I would use http_build_query to handle sanitation. My assumption, before I started investigating more closely, was that Cake would handle sanitation in the same way. If you want to use the '@' syntax, there needs to be a way for me to make user-inputted strings safe. I don't see a mechanism allowing for any sort of sanitation.

The discussion regarding the change to php-curl can be found here:

https://wiki.php.net/rfc/curl-file-upload
I'm not sure we can _remove_ the feature in a bugfix release. We could deprecate it now with warnings and remove the `@` syntax in a future release and recommending people use file handles instead.

That's a valid concern, for sure. I take it from your shift in focus that you share my concerns at this point?

I kind of doubt that many people are using such an obscure feature of a brand new release (I'm not aware of an equivalent in Cake 2.x), but I suppose it's better to do it right.

Some sort of real sanitization does need to be added as a stopgap, though. `ltrim($foo,"@")` doesn't cut it. Unfortunately, belatedly adding escaping may do more damage than good. Backslash escaping would require backslashes to be escaped as well, which may do more collateral damage than dropping `@` support immediately would. Adding escaping to the mix also makes things even messier when it's no longer needed.

Three options come to mind:
- Interpret `"@myfile"` as `fopen("myfile","r")` and `"@@mystring"` as `"@mystring"`. I'm not a big fan of this as it's not exactly intuitive, but it's probably the least destructive you can get with the sanitization option.
- Accept string as well as array input in the second field, allowing users to use `http_build_query()` to construct a safe query string to pass to the function. This is probably the cleanest option.
- As was done with php-curl, add a configuration option to disable the functionality, defaulting first to enabled, then to disabled, then removed.

I should mention that I don't mind making any of the above changes myself, assuming there's community support for them.

Accepting a string for request body data might be the simplest way to sidestep the issue for those who want to take arbitrary user data and use it in a subsequent request. I agree that adding escaping will only complicate matters both now and later.

I think if we deprecate with an `E_DEPRECATED` warning and recommend people use strings when accepting untrusted data we can consider removing the '@' syntax in a future release.

Sending a string payload should already work, if the content-type is set. However, we could smooth over a missing content-type by defaulting to `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.
I didn't test get(), I only looked at post() which did support string data.
Yes, the other methods seem to work fine, so long as the `Content-type` header is explicitly specified. Hence the condition in my code snippet.
I can put together a pull request tonight to add the default content-types and deprecation warnings.

issue.title: Make Http\Client File uploads safer and better

repository.name: cakephp
repository.description: CakePHP: The Rapid Development Framework for PHP - Official Repository

issue.body:
The @ is not a completely safe way to send files. If a developer passes along user data, that user data can include arbitrary files. This is not desirable, and can go really wrong with URLs.

This also improves content-type and filename detection for local stream resources and request bodies that are strings.

Refs #6540
